title: The Opposition
subtitle: The king duel that decides pawn endings.
goals: Steal the opposition with a pawn tempo

steps.say: When two kings face each other with one square between them, neither may step forward — so whoever must move first has to give way. Having your opponent on move in that stand-off is called HAVING THE OPPOSITION, and it decides most king-and-pawn endings. It's the closest thing chess has to a staring contest.

steps.prompt: Step up and TAKE the opposition!
hints: Move so the kings face each other with exactly one square between — with BLACK to move.
Straight forward: after Kd4, Black faces you and must be the one to blink.

line.say: Face to face, one square apart, Black to move — YOU have the opposition. Whatever Black does now, he steps aside and your king advances past him.

rejections.say: A sidestep — no confrontation, no gain. The opposition is taken by facing the enemy king directly with HIM to move: Kd4.

steps.wrongSay: Put your king directly in front of Black's, one square away, so that Black must move first.
steps.successSay: The staring contest is won by arriving second. Position first, then let them blink.

steps.prompt: You're BLACK, defending a pawn down. Exactly one move draws — the defensive opposition!
hints: White's king is one square ahead of its pawn — that wins ONLY if White gets the opposition. Deny it!
Face the white king directly: king to e7, and White can never make progress.

line.say: The only move! Kings face off with WHITE to move — you have the opposition. Now you mirror every step: Kd5, Kd7! Kf5, Kf7! The pawn can advance but the king can never clear its path. Draw.

rejections.say: One square too shy! White plays Ke6! seizing the opposition, and outflanks: your king gets pushed off the queening path square by square. Only DIRECT opposition — Ke7 — holds the draw.
Kd6! White grabs the opposition and shoulders through — the pawn walks home behind the king. Face him head-on with Ke7.

steps.wrongSay: Meet the white king face to face, one square apart, with White to move. There's exactly one square that does it.
steps.successSay: Down a pawn, dead drawn — because you knew one word: opposition. This defense saves countless half-points.

steps.prompt: The kings are locked and it's YOUR move — Black has the opposition. Steal it back with the endgame's oldest trick!
hints: If your king moves, Black mirrors forever. You need to pass the turn... and kings can't pass. Who can?
The pawn! A quiet pawn step changes nothing on the board except WHOSE TURN it is.

line.say: The spare tempo! Same king stand-off — but now BLACK must move...
...and you outflank immediately. The pawn 'wasted' a move so your king wouldn't have to. Tempo is a currency: the side with a spare pawn move is rich.

rejections.say: Kd7! — mirrored. Kf5, Kf7! — mirrored again. The king dance never ends because Black holds the opposition. Only a PAWN move can pass the turn back to Black.
Kf7! Black keeps the mirror going forever. You must lose a move to win the game — and only the pawn can lose one for you.

steps.wrongSay: Any king move gets mirrored. Find the move that keeps the position but flips the turn.
steps.successSay: Losing a move to win the game — the deepest little paradox in chess, and now it's yours.

steps.prompt: You're BLACK against the dreaded ROOK pawn. There's a fortress that saves you — run to it!
hints: Rook pawns are the great exception: the defender draws if his king reaches the corner — no opposition needed!
Head straight for c8, b8, a8. In the corner, White's only ways to make progress are stalemate. That's a draw.

line.say: Straight to the corner! Once your king touches c8–b8–a8, nothing evicts it: every White try ends in stalemate. Rook pawns can't outflank — there's no other side of the board to use.
On the road to c8 and the corner fortress — where the a-pawn's dreams go to die. Against rook pawns, the corner is an automatic draw.

rejections.say: Chasing the pawn from behind loses the race: Kb6! and White's king seizes the front, shepherding the pawn home. Run to the CORNER — the one fortress that never falls.

steps.wrongSay: Against a rook pawn, forget fancy opposition — just get your king to the queening corner.
steps.successSay: The rook-pawn corner fortress: the exception that saves 'hopeless' endings. Check for it before you ever resign a pawn ending!
